name: Kingdom of Portugal (John III)

areaKm2.note: world_1530 Portugal polygon = 93,126 km2 on the sphere (metropolitan Portugal, ~92,000 km2 modern). Overseas forts not included.

population.note: HYDE via OWID: Portugal 1,147,012 (1500), 1,835,219 (1600); interpolation gives ~1.5M for 1550. Census-based estimates for 1527-32 (numeramento) ~1.2-1.4M. Mid 1.4M. Overseas Portuguese (perhaps 10,000-15,000 in Asia) excluded from the count.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share (de Vries based): Portugal 13.8% (1500), 12.7% (1600). Lisbon alone held ~100,000.

activePersonnel.note: No standing army at home before the ordenancas of 1570. Counted: soldados of the Estado da India ~6,000-10,000 (Boxer, The Portuguese Seaborne Empire, ch. 3, gives at most ~10,000 able-bodied Portuguese in Asia in the mid-16th c.), garrisons of the Moroccan fortresses (Ceuta, Tangier, Mazagao, Arzila to 1550) ~4,000, royal guard and fortress garrisons at home ~1,000, plus ~5,000-7,000 sailors and gunners of the India armadas and Indian Ocean squadrons.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: noble retinues, military orders and town levies callable within a month (the 1578 Alcacer Quibir army of ~17,000 Portuguese needed a year of raising and mercenaries).

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: sailors and gunners of the carreira da India and the Indian Ocean fleets (5-7 India ships a year, Portuguese India Armadas article, plus ~20-40 armed ships in Asia).

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: the 1578 Moroccan expedition (~17,000 Portuguese plus mercenaries, ~1.2% of population) nearly exhausted the kingdom; 3% is the practical ceiling with town and noble levies.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Soldados (arquebusiers and pikemen) in Asian fortresses (Goa, Malacca, Hormuz, Diu, Cochin) and North African garrisons; see activePersonnel note.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: arquebus and pike, superior to most Asian and Moroccan opponents

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: experienced but unorganised companies, no regimental system

count.note: Educated guess: fidalgo men-at-arms in the Moroccan fortresses.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: lance and plate

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: frontier raiding experience

count.note: Educated guess: ginete light horse of the Moroccan presidios (the fronteiros).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: jinete light horse

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: constant frontier raiding

count.note: Educated guess: field pieces outside fortress and ship mountings; Portuguese gunnery was concentrated on ships and forts.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: bronze guns from Lisbon and Goa foundries

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: contract gunners, many German and Flemish

count.note: Educated guess: carracks and galleons able to fight in line, in the India run (5-7 sailings a year, ~400 tons average, a few 900-ton ships in the 1550s: Portuguese India Armadas article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_India_Armadas) and the Goa and Malacca squadrons.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: large heavily-gunned carracks and galleons outclassed Indian Ocean opponents (Diu 1509)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: oceanic navigation and gunnery the best of the 1550s

count.note: Educated guess: caravels, fustas and galliots of the Asian and Moroccan coasts.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: lateen caravels, local fustas

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: experienced crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5 (competent, average). Evidence: capable viceroys (Joao de Castro, Diu 1546) but no permanent army command or staff

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.25-0.5. Evidence: companies of fidalgos and adventurers bound by personal loyalty

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: crusading ethos and recent victories (second siege of Diu 1546)

weapons.note: Anchor: 5 (1600: arquebus/musket, pike, field cannon). Evidence: arquebus-armed soldados, no musket or formed pike regiments yet

armor.note: Anchor: 4.7 between plate-and-mail and half-armor. Evidence: corselets and morions

ships.note: Anchor: 5 (galleons). Evidence: oceanic carracks and early galleons with broadside guns; the era leader in ocean navigation

fortification.note: Anchor: 4.6 toward 5 (trace italienne). Evidence: Mazagao (1541-42) one of the first bastioned forts outside Italy; Asian forts mostly older

logistics.note: Anchor: 4.6. Evidence: seaborne supply of fortress garrisons via the carreira da India

communications.note: Anchor: 4.6. Evidence: annual fleets; a letter Lisbon-Goa took 6-8 months

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

air.note: No aircraft or military balloons before 1783/1794.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: the crown spent most pepper-trade and customs revenue on fleets and fortresses; Moroccan forts were abandoned 1541-50 because of cost.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: shipbuilding at the Ribeira das Naus, textiles, salt.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: Portugal was a chronic grain importer (Baltic, Moroccan and Azorean wheat); Lisbon depended on imports.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: unpaved royal roads; coastal and river shipping carried most traffic.

majorPorts.note: Lisbon, Porto, Setubal, Lagos, Viana, Aveiro; overseas Goa, Malacca, Hormuz, Mozambique as bases.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: India carracks (~400 tons each, 5-7 sailings a year), Brazil and Atlantic island shipping, coastal trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: land operations limited to fortress hinterlands; sea supply carried expeditions thousands of km.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: mules, oxen and horses for 1.4M people.

homeDefense.note: 1.1 row: familiar terrain and local supply; Elvas and border castles, but 1580 showed the kingdom fell in weeks.

notes: Snapshot = 1550, late reign of John III, height of the Estado da India before the Spanish union. Population counts metropolitan Portugal only; overseas forts are basesAbroad. Personnel convention: salaried soldados in Asia and the Moroccan garrisons and fleet crews are active; noble retinues and town levies are trainedReserves (the ordenancas militia was only created in 1570). Force numbers are thin: there was no standing army and no muster series, so most counts are grade D.
